analysis.one_liner: Repeals tax breaks for oil companies and sends households a $500 gas-price rebate.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from May 2022 until the 117th Congress ended, with 3 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal a series of federal tax breaks for oil and gas companies, including deductions for drilling costs, percentage depletion, the enhanced oil recovery credit, the marginal well credit, and LIFO accounting for the biggest integrated oil companies. It would use the tax code to send every eligible household a one-time 2022 gas prices rebate: $500 per person ($1,000 per couple) plus $500 for each dependent age 16 or older, paid in advance like a stimulus check. The bill was referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Households: every eligible taxpayer with a Social Security number would get a refundable one-time payment of $500 ($1,000 on a joint return) plus $500 per dependent 16 or older, with advance payments so families got money during 2022's gas price spike, and an outreach program to reach people who do not normally file returns. Taxpayers generally gain from the revenue raised by ending oil and gas tax preferences.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a 2022 gas prices rebate of $500 per taxpayer ($1,000 for joint returns) plus $500 for each dependent age 16 or older, refundable so households owing no income tax still receive it, with advance payments made during 2022 [S2, S3].

Repeals or limits long-standing oil and gas tax preferences, including expensing of intangible drilling costs, percentage depletion, the enhanced oil recovery credit, the marginal well credit, the tertiary injectants deduction, the passive-loss exception for working interests, the qualified business income deduction for oil and gas activities, and LIFO accounting for major integrated oil companies (those producing at least 500,000 barrels a day with over $1 billion in gross receipts) [S2, S3].

Tightens the foreign tax credit for 'dual capacity' taxpayers, closing a route oil companies use to reduce US tax on foreign oil and gas income, and clarifies that tar sands and oil shale count as crude oil for excise tax purposes so they pay into the oil spill liability fund [S3].
Requires the Treasury to run an outreach program so people who do not normally file returns learn how to claim the rebate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies bear the direct cost: they would lose a set of long-standing tax preferences worth billions. The federal Treasury also bears the cost of the rebate checks beyond what the repealed tax breaks raise. To the extent companies pass some lost tax advantages through to prices, drivers could pay slightly more at the pump.

drawbacks.text: The repeal of tax preferences could raise production costs, and some of that cost could be passed through to consumers as higher fuel prices, softening the rebate's benefit during a period of high gas prices [S2, S3].

Despite the CRS description targeting 'large oil companies,' several provisions, such as repealing percentage depletion and the marginal well credit, apply to all oil and gas producers, so small and independent producers and royalty owners would lose tax treatment they currently rely on, and some advocates argue this accelerates the decline of marginal US wells [S2, S3].

The rebate is a flat one-time payment with no income limits, so high-income households receive the same $500, and its benefit to families is temporary rather than a lasting change in energy costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households, the upside is concrete and immediate: $500 to $1,000 or more in cash during a gas price spike, refundable and paid in advance. The costs fall mainly on oil and gas producers, with the risk of some pass-through to fuel prices and a hit to small producers. The design is simple and the targeting toward households is broad rather than means-tested, which is a fair trade-off to argue about but a net gain for most working families if enacted.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald McEachin introduced the bill on May 24, 2022 with Reps. Casten and Blumenauer; it had 3 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support [S1, S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day; the committee held no markup, no hearing, and never reported the bill, and the full House never voted on it [S5].
No further action was recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill lapsed and would have had to be reintroduced from scratch [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept every tax preference the bill would have repealed, and households never received the rebate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies that kept their tax breaks

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill repeals or limits roughly a dozen tax preferences they currently use, including drilling cost expensing, percentage depletion, the enhanced oil recovery credit, and LIFO accounting for the largest integrated producers. Its industry interest in keeping those preferences ran against households' interest in the rebate and in tax revenue.

industries.industry: Tar sands and oil shale producers
industries.note: The bill would classify tar sands and oil shale output as crude oil for excise tax purposes, making them pay per-barrel taxes into the oil spill liability fund, and would let regulators bring similar feedstocks into the tax. A modest added cost, partly offset by clarity about liability rules.

industries.industry: Small oil and gas producers and royalty owners
industries.note: Provisions like repealing percentage depletion and the marginal well credit are not limited to large companies, so smaller operators would lose tax treatment central to marginal well economics. The bill's framing targets big oil, but some of the revenue would come from smaller players.
